source: Farmer field-trial case study presentation, 'Rice Husk Charcoal (Angkam) Production Technique and Experimentation on Rice Cultivation' (ធ្យូងអង្កាម: បច្ចេកទេសដុតអង្កាម និងការពិសោធន៍លើដំណាំស្រូវ), documenting farmer Ms. Sang Serey of Antong Raveang village, Borribor district, Kampong Chhnang province, who has collaborated with an agricultural service organization since 2009 and currently also collaborates with the 'BCR' project; publisher/ministry and exact presentation date are not stated on the slides, no elibrary URL visible.
text:
Rice husk charcoal (in Khmer: ធ្យូងអង្កាម, 'thyung angkam') is charcoal made by burning rice husk (paddy hull, 'angkam'). The burning process breaks the husk down into small, dark, slightly sticky/clumped pieces of charcoal. This husk charcoal is used as a soil amendment in agricultural work, including preparing soil for planting and other cultivation purposes.

Benefits of using rice husk charcoal in farming, as described in the presentation: it strongly benefits agricultural work in several ways. It helps plant growth and increases yield. It helps retain soil fertility and prevents nutrients from being washed away (reduces erosion/leaching). It reduces the need for chemical fertilizer, which in turn reduces environmental damage. It helps the soil retain moisture, giving the soil better water absorption and greater resistance to drought. It can improve overall soil quality/structure. It increases populations of beneficial organisms (insects/microorganisms) living in the soil.

Equipment and technique for producing husk charcoal: the method shown uses a simple metal cylinder (an open-ended corrugated metal tube, acting as a central chimney/flue) that is set upright and partly buried or planted at a spot. Rice husk is then piled up and mounded around the cylinder in a cone shape, covering it, and the husk is set alight from inside the cylinder. The husk smolders and burns slowly (a smoldering/pyrolysis burn rather than an open flame), producing visible smoke as it carbonizes. Farmers and helpers gather around the pile during the burning process. Once the burn is complete, the husk has been converted into black rice husk charcoal, which is then collected (e.g., into baskets) for use as a soil amendment.

Note: this technique and its stated benefits are farmer/extension-project material describing a low-cost, low-technology method suitable for smallholder rice farmers to produce their own soil-amendment charcoal from a byproduct (rice husk) they already have access to.
